ABSTRACT

GENERAL TACTICAL STRATEGY

A practical field guide to building a flexible battle group, creating a reliable information advantage, coordinating detection and fire, and deciding when the battle calls for an offensive assault or disciplined defensive control.

This guide preserves the tactical framework of its source: a role-based baseline composition, replacement planning, an opening-to-endgame battle plan, target priority, a coordinated push, a defensive hold, shared concealment and crossfire rules, and a final comparison of the two principal win conditions. Its purpose is to help players understand not only where ships should go, but why their positions, consumables, firing angles, and timing must support one another.

The governing tactical principle is simple: information must become a team advantage. Spotting without guns ready, radar without a focus call, damage without a useful position, and aggression without an exit route can all waste the very resources that make a battle winnable. Build around roles first, connect those roles through communication, and commit only when the local situation supports the objective.

REFERENCE STANDARD FOR EXAMPLES

Tier X is used as the common reference point for ship-role comparisons and numerical examples, so that the named ships and capabilities can be considered on a consistent basis. This is a reference convention only: it does not restrict YOLO battles to that tier. The Admiralty may select any ship tier and event configuration; the ships, lineups, and statistics in this guide illustrate tactical principles rather than impose tournament requirements.

The guide's tactical examples are designed to be adapted to the selected event configuration, available roster, map, battle size, and bot arrangement. A sound plan is one that covers the required roles and can change when the battlefield changes.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Competitive battle strategy at a glance

THE CENTRAL PRINCIPLE

Build roles. Create information. Concentrate fire. Preserve choices.

Do not select ships merely because they are individually powerful. Build a group that can scout safely, control objectives, reveal targets, create crossfires, apply pressure, and disengage when the position becomes unfavorable.

1 · General battle system

Scout the enemy setup without paying an unnecessary health cost. Support a primary objective with vision, radar, and ready guns. Separate firing angles, focus the target that matters most, and let the score determine whether to advance or preserve control.

2 · Offensive assault

Use a coordinated objective group and a supporting fire group. Conceal the approach, force the enemy to react, create a local advantage, and commit to one objective only when allies can cover the advance and the assault group has an exit.

3 · Defensive control

Hold the territory that matters rather than every lane. Preserve ships, deny enemy capture attempts through low-cost resets, maintain useful crossfires, and make the opponent expose itself to regain points or position.

4 · Decide and adapt

Push when a local numerical or positional advantage can be converted into a kill or territory. Hold when owned objectives and safe firing positions can protect the lead. Change plans when score, time, ship losses, or enemy positioning makes the current win condition insufficient.

YOLO CONTEXT

YOLO battles use teams to conduct each battle, but the tournament is ordinarily centered on individual performance. The default draft is random, combinations may change between games, and team wins or losses usually have little or no influence on individual advancement or standings. Damage is the default scoring identity, but the selected event may reward other metrics.

Tier X remains the comparison reference for the ship examples; it does not limit the tiers that may be selected for YOLO battles.

Before battle: confirm the published configuration and roles.During battle: turn detection into coordinated fire.At the decision point: take territory or preserve control—do not drift between plans.

PART I · GENERAL TACTICAL STRATEGY

1. Recommended baseline lineup

The baseline composition combines forward information, layered radar, close-range control, sustained damage, and mobile crossfire. It is a role framework for a battle—not a fixed lineup for every map, participant count, or event.

Ohio · Battleship anchor

Provide central fire support, punish broadside targets, support a controlled push, and finish low-health enemies. Keep Ohio positioned to threaten more than one lane instead of committing immediately to a single flank. Make opponents pay when they maneuver under friendly radar and crossfire.

Gdańsk · Forward control and radar pressure

Contest approaches, threaten enemy destroyers, provide forward information, and create short radar windows for concentrated fire. Pressure the enemy's ability to operate near a cap; do not rush into the cap simply to trade away health.

Daring · Cap control

Spot, contest capture points, use smoke and hydro defensively, and threaten close-range destroyer engagements. It complements Gdańsk by helping secure an objective while Gdańsk applies radar pressure or shifts to another angle. Save smoke when it may be needed to survive a counter-push.

Petropavlovsk (Petro) · Radar anchor

Support the contested cap with radar, punish cruisers with AP, and hold a position from which allies can shoot revealed targets. Call the target before activating its relatively brief radar. A revealed enemy near an objective should face several allied guns, not Petro alone.

Role assignment comes before ship selection. Each pick should solve a team problem: forward vision, objective control, detection, sustained pressure, close-range threat, or a reliable way to disengage.
GENERAL TACTICAL STRATEGY · YOLO BATTLES4 / 26
PART I · GENERAL TACTICAL STRATEGY

Baseline lineup: complementary roles and flexibility

Napoli · Close-range support

Support a controlled advance, pressure enemy cruisers, and exploit openings when the enemy defensive position weakens. Its durability and exhaust smoke make it useful for planned close-range engagements or repositioning. Its presence should make an enemy hesitate before retaking an objective.

Venezia · Mobile crossfire

Create a second firing angle, punish exposed ships with SAP, kite under focus, and disengage using mobility and exhaust smoke. Find an angle that makes enemy cruisers turn broadside to Ohio, Petro, or Hindenburg. Prevent the team from becoming a predictable line firing from one direction.

Hindenburg · Sustained damage and kiting

Maintain dependable damage at range, protect the withdrawal route, and punish enemies chasing an isolated flank. Keep pressure up through prolonged fights rather than trading all its health for an early damage spike. Help punish an enemy that overextends.

Why the lineup works

  • Two sources of forward destroyer pressure: Gdańsk threatens with radar; Daring supplies close-range cap control. The group has options if one destroyer is forced away or loses health.
  • Layered detection: Gdańsk and Petro can reveal targets while Ohio and the cruisers exploit the information.
  • Multiple firing angles: Venezia creates mobile crossfire while Ohio, Petro, and Hindenburg pressure from different positions.
  • Push and withdrawal options: Ohio and Napoli can anchor an advance; Venezia and Hindenburg can keep pressure from safer angles.
  • No automatic all-in: the group does not need to commit every ship to the same close-range fight.
YOLO BATTLE GROUPS

The seven-ship arrangement is a role map, not a requirement that every match contain seven human participants. YOLO configurations may use different numbers of humans and bots. Bots generally fill vacant positions unless the Admiralty selects otherwise; their behavior may be moving or stationary, and the event settings determine whether stationary bots fire. With fewer human players, combine duties deliberately; with more participants, distribute duties without creating gaps or isolating a ship.

Random drafting is the normal starting arrangement, so do not depend on a permanent roster's habits. The final roster is generally confirmed around one hour before matches; the selected event settings should also be published at least one hour before play. Establish the caller, cap assignments, radar timing, focus-fire expectations, and withdrawal routes before the engagement develops.

2. Replacement planning

The Admiralty's selected event configuration determines which ships may be used. There are no permanent ship restrictions by default, but an individual YOLO event may impose ship limits, grouped restrictions, or outright bans. Restrictions may affect ships such as Napoli, Petropavlovsk, Des Moines, Moskva, Småland, and Gdańsk. Check the published event configuration before finalizing the battle lineup.

If unavailablePossible replacementTactical adjustment
OhioMontana or another suitable battleshipFavor a stronger long-range or broadside-punishing role suited to the map.
GdańskVampire II or YueyangAccount for reduced radar pressure; make the cruiser's radar plan more important.
DaringVampire II or MarceauVampire II emphasizes cap control; Marceau emphasizes mobile gun pressure.
PetropavlovskMoskva, Des Moines, or Salem, when permittedRework radar timing, firing position, and positional commitment.
NapoliHindenburg or Marseille, when permittedExpect less of Napoli's distinctive close-range toughness and smoke utility.
VeneziaHindenburg or another mobile cruiserPreserve a reliable crossfire and withdrawal plan.
HindenburgDes Moines or Salem for island control; another suitable long-range cruiser on open mapsAdapt how the group holds positions and sustains pressure.
ROSTER RULE

Replace the missing job, not merely the missing ship. Another destroyer may scout and contest caps if Gdańsk is unavailable, but the group must deliberately compensate for the lost radar pressure. A replacement changes the plan; it should not be treated as a perfect copy of the original ship.

Before the match, identify which tactical capability has been lost and assign that responsibility elsewhere. If the replacement cannot reproduce the original capability, change the engagement plan rather than pretending the same sequence will still work.

3. General battle plan: from opening to midgame

Opening — Learn the enemy setup safely

  • Use both destroyers to identify enemy positions and establish safe cap approaches.
  • Do not send both destroyers into the same capture area.
  • Keep Petro near a firing position that supports the primary cap.
  • Hold Ohio where it can threaten more than one lane.
  • Objective: discover the enemy setup without losing a destroyer or sacrificing substantial health for little gain.

Control — Choose and support an objective

  • Select a primary cap and support it with destroyer vision, radar coverage, and cruiser fire.
  • Use the second destroyer to screen a neighboring route or contest another objective without becoming isolated.
  • Do not trade a destroyer for capture progress without a clear reason.
  • Consider interrupting the enemy's capture attempt with detection and fire, then taking the objective after defensive consumables have been spent.

Damage — Make radar windows count

  • Before radar is activated, the caller announces the likely target and focus.
  • Destroyers and cruisers should be ready to shoot before the target is revealed.
  • Once spotted, every ship with a realistic firing solution prioritizes the target.
  • Do not use radar merely because an enemy might be nearby. Use it when the reveal can cause meaningful damage, force a retreat, or deny an objective.

Midgame — Build crossfires

  • Arrange cruisers on different firing axes once enemy positions are understood.
  • Venezia: seek a flank that forces enemy ships to turn.
  • Hindenburg: maintain sustained pressure.
  • Petro: hold the key threat zone.
  • Ohio: punish exposed targets.
  • Avoid placing every cruiser behind the same island or in the same firing lane. A one-direction formation lets enemies angle against most of the group.

PART I · GENERAL TACTICAL STRATEGY

4. Decision point, endgame, and target priority

Decision point — Push only with support

A coordinated advance becomes more attractive when the enemy has lost a ship; a key enemy is low enough to finish; important enemy radar or smoke is unavailable; or the enemy formation has been split and cannot bring its guns to bear. Do not push simply because Ohio or Napoli is healthy. Advance when allies can support the move and the enemy cannot punish it with concentrated crossfire.

Endgame — When ahead

  • Avoid unnecessary health trades.
  • Keep a ship spotting.
  • Preserve radar for a likely contest.
  • Make the enemy cross dangerous firing lanes to recover.

Endgame — When behind

  • Rally around one achievable objective.
  • Isolate one enemy and concentrate fire to create a temporary numerical advantage.
  • Use torpedoes to constrain retreat routes where appropriate.
  • Do not feed ships into the enemy formation one at a time.

5. Target priority

Use this as a default decision order, not an inflexible rule:

  1. A spotted enemy destroyer that can be hit. Removing enemy spotting and cap pressure can change the battle.
  2. A low-health radar cruiser or other high-impact support ship. Removing detection and crossfire threats makes the next move safer.
  3. Any exposed ship that can be eliminated with the available salvoes. Secure a kill rather than spreading damage across several targets.
  4. Battleships and other durable targets when a finish is realistic or their presence blocks the next objective.

Override the list when necessary: a battleship showing a fatal broadside or a nearly dead cruiser about to escape may be the urgent target. Focus the ship whose removal creates the greatest immediate tactical advantage.

PART I · GENERAL TACTICAL STRATEGY

5. Understanding the competitive objective

The battle's tactical win condition and the participant's tournament objective are related, but they are not automatically the same thing.

YOLO is ordinarily an individual-performance competition. Players form teams to conduct each battle, but drafting is normally random and may change between games or event evenings. By default, team victories and defeats have little or no influence on an individual's bracket movement, seeding, or final standing. The event configuration may deliberately include team results, but that influence must be selected and defined rather than assumed.

Damage is the default scoring identity. An event may instead, or additionally, select potential damage, kills, torpedo hits, XP, credits, survival, objective performance, or a combination of measures. Different rounds can use different formulas. The participant should know which metric is being rewarded before the match begins, because the scoring objective changes which tactical contributions are most valuable.

Damage-focused

Preserve firing uptime, create reliable angles, punish exposed targets, and stay alive long enough to deliver sustained damage. Do not mistake low-value farming for progress toward the battle win condition.

Potential-damage-focused

Use durable, useful pressure to attract fire while remaining in a position to disengage. Drawing attention is not a reason to sit in an unmanageable crossfire or spend the ship's health without purpose.

Kill-focused

Coordinate focus fire, call low-health targets, and finish ships whose removal changes spotting, radar, objective control, or the enemy's ability to support a flank.

Objective-focused

Prioritize vision, capture control, resets, safe contesting, and survival. A ship that denies an enemy capture or holds a decisive approach may be more valuable than one that deals damage from an irrelevant position.

Combined metrics

Understand which measures are included and how the chosen event combines them. Do not assume that every damaging action, cap action, or kill is weighted equally.

TACTICAL APPLICATION

Play the battle correctly while understanding what the tournament is counting. Do not abandon an essential team role to chase a personal number, and do not assume that winning the battle automatically determines an individual's tournament standing. Know the selected metric, execute the team plan, and produce the strongest individual performance that the situation allows.

PART II · OFFENSIVE ASSAULT / PUSH

1. Purpose and win condition

Goal: take a neutral or enemy cap, establish a close-range threat, and eliminate opponents through local superiority and decisive kills.

  • Take territory instead of relying on a long kite to reset capture progress later.
  • Force the enemy to fight on unfavorable terms.
  • Commit only when positioning, numbers, support, and consumables make the engagement favorable.
  • A push is not a straight-line charge. Concealment, crossfire awareness, timing, and an exit route still matter.

Illustrative seven-ship assault composition

Schlieffen · Primary brawler

Secondaries, torpedoes, hydro, and speed create a dangerous close-range threat. Its relatively small health pool and limited Repair Party charges make an unsupported early push costly. Do not let an early salvo reveal the plan before support is ready.

Napoli · Secondary brawler

High survivability, strong secondaries, and exhaust smoke support the close-range advance. Use smoke for a planned engagement, reposition, or withdrawal—not as a substitute for an exit plan.

Gdańsk · Radar pressure

Use radar to reveal an enemy destroyer when the group can concentrate fire. Radar duration is short; target calls and allied readiness matter more than pressing the consumable on suspicion.

Daring · Cap fighter

Screen the advance, contest the chosen cap, and add a second torpedo threat. Stay slightly ahead of or offset from the heavier ships, but within supporting gun range. Provide early warning as well as objective control.

GENERAL TACTICAL STRATEGY · YOLO BATTLES10 / 26
PART II · OFFENSIVE ASSAULT / PUSH

Assault lineup and two supporting groups

Marseille · Mobile assault

Speed, reload booster, and flanking pressure threaten enemies from a different angle. Exploit a developing fight rather than being the first ship to reveal itself. Shift into a firing position when enemies turn toward Schlieffen and Napoli.

Petropavlovsk · Radar support

Support the push from a protected angle rather than brawling alongside Schlieffen. Use radar and heavy AP to punish exposed or broadside targets.

Hindenburg · Sustained damage and torpedo threat

Supply sustained gun pressure; hydro and torpedoes make confined approaches dangerous. Its detectability and limited speed mean it should not lead the advance.

2. Formation: two supporting groups

Group A — Objective assault

Schlieffen + Napoli + Daring

  • Daring scouts and contests the route.
  • Napoli advances through cover with Schlieffen.
  • The two heavy ships should enter effective engagement range at roughly the same stage of the battle.

Group B — Fire support and crossfire

Gdańsk + Petropavlovsk + Marseille + Hindenburg

  • Gdańsk and Petro provide radar pressure.
  • Hindenburg supplies sustained damage.
  • Marseille searches for an offset firing angle.
  • This group should make it difficult for the enemy to focus all fire on the assault group.

Spacing rule: keep both groups close enough to support each other. An offset angle is useful; a gap that lets the enemy defeat one group before the other can intervene is not.

PART II · OFFENSIVE ASSAULT / PUSH

3. How to execute the push: approach and force a reaction

01

Approach without revealing the plan

  • Use islands, concealment, and map edges to mask the approach.
  • Avoid firing at maximum range if it reveals Schlieffen before the group is ready.
  • Gdańsk and Daring identify the opposition and report likely crossfire lanes.
  • Keep the heavy ships outside the worst incoming firing angles until the enemy's support relationships are understood.
02

Force a reaction

  • Use a radar window to threaten an enemy destroyer or discourage a cap contest.
  • Meanwhile, Marseille and Hindenburg establish angles that punish enemies who turn toward Schlieffen.
  • Look for an isolated enemy, a spent defensive consumable, a low-health target, or a flank that cannot support the rest of the enemy group.
Timing matters more than the first shot. A premature salvo can reveal the assault before supporting ships have their positions. Make the enemy react to a threat that the full group is already prepared to exploit.
GENERAL TACTICAL STRATEGY · YOLO BATTLES12 / 26
PART II · OFFENSIVE ASSAULT / PUSH

Commit, convert, and check the conditions

03

Commit to one objective

  • Take a neutral or enemy cap and win the local fight.
  • Focus the enemy destroyer or vulnerable support ship that can be killed; do not spread damage across all seven opponents.
  • Schlieffen and Napoli move in when the support group can prevent the enemy from safely focusing them.
  • Launch torpedoes to punish predictable retreats, deny a narrow approach, or finish an enemy—not as a reason to expose broadside to several guns.
04

Turn a local win into territory

  • After gaining a ship advantage, secure the cap and pressure the next objective while the enemy reorganizes.
  • Do not automatically fall back to kite and reset a cap you already own if a favorable fight can win another objective.
  • Assign a ship to screen routes threatening existing caps; the other six can sustain pressure if the screen is adequate.
  • If the enemy can win the point race by completing a capture, defending that cap takes priority over chasing kills.

4. Push checklist: green lights and red lights

Green lights — Conditions that support a hard push

  • The enemy destroyer is located, or its route is understood.
  • The group can focus fire on one or more targets.
  • The main enemy crossfire is masked, occupied, or otherwise manageable.
  • The assault group has a viable exit route.

Red lights — Conditions to delay or cancel

  • Schlieffen is spotted before its support is ready.
  • Multiple enemy firing angles cover the approach.
  • Friendly radar cannot be coordinated with allied guns.
  • A forward ship is already too low on health to survive or be rescued.

Remember: the secondaries are not the problem; the timing is. Schlieffen and Napoli are most dangerous after the group sets up the engagement. Close-range weapons do not make them immune to crossfire or concentrated AP.

PART II · OFFENSIVE ASSAULT / PUSH

5. Offensive alternatives and role compensation

The assault composition must remain adaptable to the ships and restrictions selected for an event. If a preferred ship is unavailable, choose a replacement based on the role that needs to be preserved and the tactical trade-off that the new ship introduces.

Missing shipPractical replacementTactical trade-off
SchlieffenSt. Vincent or OhioSt. Vincent retains torpedo threat and mobility; Ohio is more of a gun-and-sustain anchor. Neither duplicates Schlieffen's secondary-focused threat.
NapoliMarseille or HindenburgMaintains pressure but loses Napoli's combination of survivability, secondaries, and exhaust smoke.
GdańskSmåland, if selected and permitted, or MarceauSmåland offers a different destroyer-control package; Marceau emphasizes gun pressure, so another ship must cover the lost radar role.
PetropavlovskMoskva, Des Moines, or Alexander Nevsky, when permittedChoose based on whether the group needs radar at range or protected island-based fire support.
MarseilleVenezia or Henri IVRetains mobility and crossfire pressure with a different damage profile and defensive toolkit.
REPLACEMENT TEST

Ask three questions: What job disappeared? Which remaining ship can cover part of it? What change to positioning or timing is needed because the replacement does not perform the same way?

The replacement is successful only when the complete battle group still has a workable plan. The answer may be to change the approach, reduce the depth of the push, delay the radar window, or let a different ship take responsibility for the objective screen.

PART III · DEFENSIVE CONTROL / HOLD

1. Purpose and win condition

Goal: preserve ships, defend the territory that matters, reset enemy capture attempts, and win through positioning and capture-point pressure.

  • You do not need to kill every enemy or own every cap at once.
  • Preserve health long enough for positional advantage and points to decide the battle.
  • Make opponents lose health whenever they try to change the situation.
  • Reset enemies contesting an owned cap instead of chasing them into a poor position.
  • Use concealment, long-range HE pressure, radar, island cover, and kiting mobility.
  • If the score makes passive defense insufficient, shift to a limited counterattack with a clear target.

Illustrative seven-ship defensive composition

Conqueror · Long-range HE and fire pressure

Long-range HE, high fire chance, and Specialized Repair Teams create sustained pressure. The source notes a 24.25 km main-battery range and 48% base HE fire chance. Its armor can suffer under sustained HE punishment; do not remain exposed in crossfire just because it can heal.

Daring · Cap defender

Watch approaches to the controlled cap. Spot when safe and contest only when support is available. Preserve smoke and health when enemy radar or gunboats can punish the position.

Shimakaze · Stealth screening

Low detectability and torpedoes provide scouting and area denial. Its information and the space enemies refuse to cross may be more valuable than damage. Avoid opening fire on a target that cannot be finished if doing so sacrifices concealment.

GENERAL TACTICAL STRATEGY · YOLO BATTLES15 / 26
PART III · DEFENSIVE CONTROL / HOLD

Defensive composition: radar, sustained fire, and mobile kiting

Alexander Nevsky · Long-range radar

The source notes a 19.04 km gun range, radar, and rapid-firing guns. Reveal targets when allied guns are ready to exploit the information. Limited survivability and poor maneuverability make an exposed position dangerous.

Hindenburg · Sustained damage

The source notes a 17.83 km range, rapid main battery, HE pressure, and hydro. Apply HE pressure to battleships and cruisers; switch to AP against suitable broadside targets. Use islands and kiting angles rather than trying to occupy Nevsky's exact position.

Henri IV · Mobile kiter

The source notes a 19.08 km range, high fire chance, speed boost, and reload booster. Use range and speed to make incoming fire harder to land; reposition when the enemy builds a crossfire. High detectability makes it better suited to distance and movement than to a close position with no escape route.

Zaō · Stealth crossfire

High accuracy, low detectability, and torpedoes threaten exposed ships from a concealed angle. Go dark and reposition when enemies turn toward it. Its small health pool makes concealment and crossfire awareness essential.

BATTLESHIP ALTERNATIVE

Montana can replace Conqueror if the group prefers a more conventional, durable gun platform. The source notes a 23.65 km base main-battery range, enhanced Repair Party, and 36% base HE fire chance. This trades Conqueror's stronger HE fire pressure and repair profile for a different defensive package.

The source's numerical ship examples are retained. A separate verification note at the end records the current listed figures checked against the World of Warships Wiki, without silently altering the tactical source.

2. Defensive positioning: hold important territory, not every lane

POSITION A

Main cap defense

Daring + Alexander Nevsky + Hindenburg

  • Daring gathers information and contests safe approaches.
  • Nevsky supplies long-range fire support and radar.
  • Hindenburg occupies a separate position to punish ships maneuvering toward the cap.
POSITION B

Range and crossfire

Conqueror + Henri IV + Zaō

  • Keep these ships at different angles to the main fight.
  • Prefer a route behind an island or terrain boundary.
  • Make enemies turn, lose health, and give up favorable positioning rather than driving directly into their formation.
POSITION C

Concealed screen

Shimakaze

  • Spot enemy movements, threaten torpedo lanes, and warn of flanking attempts.
  • Do not force it to fight an enemy gunboat merely to maintain vision if losing it would remove the group's forward information.

3. How to execute the hold — Step 1

01

Choose a defensible two-cap plan

  • Assign two ships to protect the primary cap and its approaches.
  • Keep the rest of the group in a support formation that can reach both important objectives.
  • Do not push deep into the third cap just because it is not yours.
  • Use islands to block at least one enemy firing axis where possible.
  • Keep enough separation for crossfires, but not so much that an enemy can isolate one ship.
GENERAL TACTICAL STRATEGY · YOLO BATTLES17 / 26
PART III · DEFENSIVE CONTROL / HOLD

How to execute the hold: concealment, resets, and endgame control

02

Preserve concealment and fire from chosen positions

  • Shimakaze and Daring provide forward vision.
  • Cruisers should fire from positions that reach targets without exposing their broadside to a second enemy angle.
  • Nevsky should use its range to create radar opportunities while avoiding an open-water position where the whole enemy group can shoot it.
  • Main-battery fire can increase a ship's sea detectability to its gun range for up to 20 seconds when enemies can spot it. Breaking line of sight behind an island can end exposure sooner.
  • Plan a cover route before firing, not after return fire begins.
03

Reset an enemy capture attempt

  • If an enemy destroyer or cruiser enters a cap you control, prioritize revealing and damaging that ship.
  • Use radar when several allied ships can shoot the target.
  • If it retreats, secure the cap instead of chasing it around an island.
  • Prefer a low-cost reset from protected positions over sacrificing multiple cruisers to stop one capture attempt.
04

Kite when the enemy commits

  • When several enemies focus one cruiser, disengage along its preplanned route while maintaining a firing angle if possible.
  • Henri IV: use speed and distance. Zaō: use concealment to go dark. Hindenburg: use island cover and hydro to protect the retreat.
  • Do not have every ship retreat in the same direction and expose broadside to the same enemy.
  • One ship can kite while another holds a protected island position, preserving overlapping fire.
05

Let points force the opponent to act

  • Once the group controls the necessary objectives, do not advance just to seek damage.
  • Use HE to start fires, punish approaches, and force Damage Control Party use.
  • Keep a destroyer spotting so the group can switch targets when an enemy becomes vulnerable.
  • If ahead on ships and points, maintain safe control.
  • If the enemy's points lead is too large to overcome by waiting, launch a limited counterattack against a clear local target.

MAP NOTE

Des Moines is especially useful when terrain protects its hull while allowing fire onto an approaching cap. Its high main-battery DPM is offset by the source-noted 15.83 km range, so it is not the default choice for open-water kiting.

A defensive composition should be judged by how well it can cover the selected objectives, preserve concealment, create supporting angles, and disengage when focused. A replacement that fits one map may be unsuitable on another. Change the formation and the range plan to fit the terrain.

REFERENCE · RULES SHARED BY BOTH STRATEGIES

Mandatory concealment and crossfire rules

These rules apply whether the group is advancing or defending. They are not separate from the plan; they are the conditions that keep either plan from collapsing under avoidable detection, crossfire, or resource mistakes.

  1. Know the likely return fire before exposing a ship.
    • Before opening fire, each cruiser should know which enemies can shoot it.
    • Identify where to go if two or more opponents turn their guns toward you.
  2. Use spotting to create a shooting advantage—not just information.
    • Radar is valuable when the group can exploit the reveal.
    • A concealed destroyer spotting a weak flank may be more useful than one that fires and loses its spotting advantage.
  3. Create your own crossfires without entering two enemy crossfires.
    • Friendly ships should use different firing angles.
    • Each ship should avoid a position where two enemy groups can hit it at once.
    • Use islands, concealment, and deliberate spacing to limit incoming guns.
  4. Treat smoke as cover, not immunity.
    • Smoke can also hide enemy ships from your group.
    • Radar, hydro, close-range detection, and torpedoes can still threaten a smoke position.
    • Every smoke deployment needs a detection plan and an exit route.
  5. Do not trade health for damage that does not advance the win condition.
    • A battleship with 40,000 HP and a useful Repair Party remaining can still shape the battle.
    • More damage dealt is not worth becoming too weak to defend or contest a decisive objective.
  6. Neither defend a cap at any cost nor abandon it for damage.
    • Decide based on score, remaining time, ship count, and whether the enemy capture can change the outcome.

REFERENCE · FINAL DECISION

Push or hold? Choose the win condition that fits the battle

This is the specific strategic comparison between the offensive assault and defensive control plans. It is different from the general opening-to-endgame framework in Part I: the general framework describes how the group operates; this comparison helps decide which win condition to pursue.

Decision factorOFFENSIVE PUSH

Primary win conditionCapture enemy territory and eliminate ships.Preserve owned caps and win through points.
Preferred engagementClose-range fight with a local advantage.Longer-range fight with a planned escape route.

Radar usageReveal a target for an immediate focus-fire window.Reveal a capper without exposing the defending group.

REFERENCE · FINAL DECISION

Quick decision guide and the final rule

Choose the push when:

  • A local numerical or positional advantage exists.
  • Enemy ships are isolated, low, or unable to support each other.
  • Radar and focus fire can create a kill window.
  • The assault group can advance without being trapped in overlapping crossfire.
  • A successful fight can secure a cap or materially improve the point race.

Choose the hold when:

  • Your group already controls the objectives needed to win.
  • Your ships have safe firing positions and planned retreat routes.
  • The enemy must cross exposed water or give up territory to contest.
  • You can reset captures without sacrificing ships.
  • Your lead can be protected by spotting, disciplined damage, and patience.

Change plans when:

  • The score makes the current plan insufficient.
  • A key ship is lost or a critical role is no longer covered.
  • The enemy's formation, consumables, or positioning changes the engagement.
  • A cap is about to decide the battle and demands immediate action.
THE FINAL RULE

General strategy is the team's operating system. Push or hold is the match-specific win condition.

Scout safely, coordinate radar, focus fire, build crossfires, preserve escape routes, and adapt to the score. Then push when a favorable local fight can win territory—or hold when disciplined positioning can make the enemy lose the point race.

FINAL TACTICAL REFERENCE

Final composition recommendation and field guide

The most complete all-purpose seven-ship example in this guide is Ohio, Gdańsk, Daring, Petropavlovsk, Napoli, Venezia, and Hindenburg, provided those ships fit the selected event configuration.

Together, they satisfy the general team framework with two complementary destroyers for scouting and cap control, layered radar, coordinated focus fire, durable support, sustained damage, and multiple crossfire angles.

General battle

Gdańsk and Daring provide forward information and cap pressure. Petro supports the primary threat zone. Ohio punishes exposed targets. Venezia and Hindenburg create alternate angles and help preserve a withdrawal route. Napoli gives the group a credible close-range option.

Offensive assault

Ohio and Napoli can support a controlled advance while Gdańsk and Petropavlovsk create brief detection windows for concentrated fire. Venezia and Hindenburg pressure from supporting angles so the enemy cannot focus every gun on the assault group.

Defensive control

Daring can help secure objectives, the radar ships can deter or expose enemy cap attempts, and Venezia and Hindenburg can kite or disengage while preserving crossfires and escape routes.

The lineup's key advantage is flexibility: it can concentrate force when a favorable push is available or spread into disciplined, mutually supporting positions when holding the lead is the better win condition. Replace any unavailable ship by role, and deliberately compensate for any lost radar, spotting, cap-control, or crossfire capability.

VISUAL TACTICAL FIELD GUIDE · PART I

General strategy and offensive assault

FIELD REFERENCE · PART I

THE BATTLE GROUP'S OPERATING SYSTEM

Information → control → coordinated fire → decision → conversion

PART I · GENERAL TEAM STRATEGY — THE FOUNDATION FOR EVERY BATTLE

1 · Early spotting and information

Find enemy positions early. Keep the map open. Share information with the group.

2 · Overlapping radar

Coordinate radar coverage. Create detection traps. Keep guns ready before a reveal.

3 · Crossfires and focus fire

Avoid firing from the same angle. Create crossfires. Eliminate targets quickly.

4 · Caps, health, and endgame

Contest and reset caps. Manage ship health and positioning. Plan for the final push or defense.

PART II · OFFENSIVE ASSAULT / PUSH

Create a local advantage and take territory.

  1. Assault group and support group: lead with the right ships, keep supporting fire, and maintain spacing and angles.
  2. Timing and commitment: strike when the enemy is vulnerable, avoid overextending, and commit as a coordinated battle group.
  3. Focus fire and kills: eliminate key targets first, use radar and spotting, and maintain fire discipline.
  4. Objective capture: secure the cap, hold until support arrives, and avoid becoming isolated.
  5. When to push / when to stop: push on advantage; stop if outnumbered or low on health; regroup and reset.
SPOT & IDENTIFY→CREATE CROSSFIRE→FOCUS FIRE→SECURE OBJECTIVE

THE ASSAULT SEQUENCE

1Mask the approach
2Radar + focus fire
3Take cap + exit

Do not reveal the brawling threat before supporting guns are ready. Convert a local kill into territory, then screen the caps already secured.

THE RIGHT SHIPS + THE RIGHT ROLESSupport range, information, and timing make an assault possible. Aggression without support is only an early trade.
GENERAL TACTICAL STRATEGY · YOLO BATTLES24 / 26
VISUAL TACTICAL FIELD GUIDE · PART II

Defensive control and shared tactical rules

FIELD REFERENCE · PART II

DEFENSIVE CONTROL & MATCH DECISIONS

Preserve ships · protect objectives · force the opponent to act

PART III · DEFENSIVE CONTROL / HOLD

Preserve ships, control territory, and manage the point race.

1 · Key caps and reset

Hold important objectives, reset enemy captures, and use smoke and hydro wisely.

2 · Safe firing positions

Maintain range and cover, keep an escape route, and avoid unnecessary risks.

3 · Escape routes

Plan the retreat, keep mobility options open, and avoid getting trapped.

4 · Force enemy mistakes

Bait overextensions, use radar and information, and punish poor positioning.

WHEN TO PUSH / WHEN TO STOP

PUSH
  • Enemy is split or weak.
  • Allies are in position.
  • Air cover or surface support is available where configured.
HOLD
  • Enemy is stronger.
  • Own ships are low on health.
  • There is no support or the position is poor.

SHARED TACTICAL RULES

Stay togetherKeep ships within supporting range.
Use radar wiselyCall targets before firing.
Manage resourcesSmoke, hydro, and HP are limited.
CommunicateShare information, call shots, stay calm.
AdaptAdjust to the enemy and the situation.

PUSH VS. HOLD · QUICK COMPARISON

FactorPushHold
HealthSpend to gain groundPreserve for later
RangeClose to mediumMedium to long
RadarCreate attack windowsProtect key areas
TorpedoesLimited / situationalDefense / area denial
